evidence: Ter. And. 762: Tibi ego dīcō, annōn?
Plaut. Men. 696: heus tū, tibi dīcō
terms.comment: With an accusative and infinitive for what is said (dīcit sē ventūrum esse) and a dative of the person told: Dīc mihi, “tell me”; Tibi dīcō!, “I’m talking to you!” The imperative is dīc.

terms.gloss: say, with the speaker’s own words
evidence: Cic. Att. 5.1.3: ēn, inquit, mihi haec ego patior cotīdiē
terms.comment: Only with direct speech, and never before it: it follows the first word or words, «Venī,» inquit, «mēcum.», or the first sentence, «Venī,» inquit. «Cēna parāta est.» After a repeated word it insists: manē, inquam, “wait, I said”.

terms.gloss: say, say yes; ajunt, they say
evidence: Ter. Eun. 252: Negat quis? negō: ait? ajō.
Ter. Ph. 419: Āctum, ajunt, nē agās.
Ter. And. 1.2.21: ita ajunt, so they say (Lewis & Short s.v. ita)
Traupman p. 107: so they say, ita ajunt
terms.comment: The opposite of negō. Ajunt, “they say”, brings in a saying; Quid ais? is “What do you say?” or “What’s that?”. For Ain' vērō? see really.

evidence: Cic. Att. 2.8.1: quaerō ecquid litterārum. negant.
terms.comment: Latin for “say that … not”: negat sē ventūrum esse, he says he won’t come.

phrases.latin: ecce tibi nūntius puerōs vēnisse Rōmā! vocō, quaerō ecquid litterārum. negant. quid ais? inquam, nihilne ā Pompōniō?
phrases.english: And look: news that the couriers have come from Rome! I call them and ask if there’s a letter. They say no. “What?” I say, “nothing from Pomponius?”
You’ll pay for it — I won’t say how.

phrases.latin: Tibi ego dīcō, annōn? … Mitte id quod sciō: dīc quod rogō.
phrases.english: I’m talking to you, aren’t I? … Never mind what I know: tell me what I’m asking.
